uncited: This family compares two distinct approaches for rendering mixtures of geometric primitives and volumetric data: hybrid ray tracing and 3D scan-conversion.

The choice between them depends on whether the application prioritizes the physical accuracy of ray-traced lighting and shadows or the structural clarity provided by scan-converted geometric backdrops.
Both methods address the problem of integrating explicit geometric primitives (such as polygons) with implicit volumetric datasets (such as CT or MRI scans) into a single coherent image.
Hybrid ray tracing renders the mixture by casting rays through the volume and intersecting them with geometric primitives using standard ray-triangle intersection tests.
Geometric primitives are treated as opaque or semi-transparent objects that cast shadows and interact with the volume's lighting.
This method is chosen when accurate lighting effects, such as shadows cast by geometric structures onto the volume, are required.
3D scan-conversion renders the mixture by first 3D scan-converting geometric primitives into the volumetric dataset.
The resulting composite ensemble is then rendered using standard volume rendering techniques.
This method is chosen when the structural clarity of the geometric primitives is paramount.

Both approaches are considered reasonably efficient for their respective use cases, though their performance profiles differ [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that both approaches are considered reasonably efficient for their respective use cases, though their performance profiles differ. The evidence in Source [S1], specifically in the 'Conclusions' section, explicitly states: 'Although both are reasonably efficient and produce images free from aliasing artifacts, each have advantages and disadvantages in terms of cost, image quality, and versatility.' This confirms that both are efficient and that they differ in aspects related to performance (cost, quality, versatility).

This confirms that tri-linear interpolation is used and that it causes blurring at polygonal edges that could be reduced with a better filter.
